title: Linux Text Processing
description: Learn powerful text manipulation tools including grep, sed, awk, cut, sort, uniq, wc, and head/tail for log analysis and data extraction.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, app.log is a readable text file. Use GNU grep to print every line containing the literal substring ERROR, matching case exactly; ERROR may occur inside a longer word.
tasks.hint: Give grep the case-sensitive pattern and file: grep ERROR app.log
tasks.explanation: grep prints lines matching its pattern. ERROR contains no regex metacharacters, so it also works with -F for literal matching. -i would include other case variants; -w would miss occurrences inside longer words.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, server.log is readable and contains at least 15 lines. Submit one complete Bash command list using GNU head then GNU tail to print its first 10 lines followed by its last 5 lines.
tasks.hint: Separate the two commands with a semicolon: head -n 10 server.log; tail -n 5 server.log
tasks.explanation: head -n 10 prints the first ten lines; tail -n 5 prints the last five. A semicolon runs both on the original file and concatenates their output. A pipe would send only the head output to tail.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, hosts.txt is a readable text file; a line may contain localhost multiple times. Use GNU sed to print the file with only the first localhost occurrence on each line replaced by 127.0.0.1. Leave the file unchanged.
tasks.hint: Use a substitution without the global flag: sed 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/' hosts.txt
tasks.explanation: sed substitutes the first match on each line by default and prints the processed text. A g flag would replace every match; -i would edit the file instead of leaving it unchanged.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, the readable file users.csv contains comma-separated records with at least three fields, no header, no quoted fields, and no embedded commas. awk is available. Use awk to print only the third field of each record.
tasks.hint: Set the comma delimiter and protect the awk program from Bash: awk -F, '{print $3}' users.csv
tasks.explanation: awk -F, splits these simple records on commas; $3 selects the third field. Single quotes pass $3 to awk unchanged. Inside double quotes, escape the dollar sign to prevent Bash from expanding its positional parameter first.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, /etc/passwd is readable and each record has colon-separated fields. Use GNU cut to print only fields 1 and 3, retaining the colon separator.
tasks.hint: Use cut with separate delimiter and field options: cut -d: -f1,3 /etc/passwd
tasks.explanation: cut -d: selects colon-separated fields; -f1,3 prints fields 1 and 3 in input order. The delimiter and field-selection options are separate arguments.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, scores.txt is readable and contains one decimal number per line; LC_ALL=C. Use GNU sort to print the numbers in descending numeric order, keeping duplicate values and leaving the file unchanged.
tasks.hint: Combine numeric and reverse ordering: sort -rn scores.txt
tasks.explanation: sort -n compares numeric values rather than the spelling of each line. -r reverses the order. Sorting writes to standard output by default; without -u, duplicate values remain.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, access.log is readable text whose identical lines are already adjacent; differences in case matter. Use GNU uniq to print each distinct line once with its occurrence count, without changing the file.
tasks.hint: Ask uniq to prefix each output line with its count: uniq -c access.log
tasks.explanation: uniq -c collapses adjacent equal lines and prefixes each with their count. This counts every occurrence here because the input already groups identical lines together. -i would wrongly merge case variants.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, document.txt is readable text and every line ends with a newline. Use GNU wc to report only the line count (the filename may accompany it), without modifying the file.
tasks.hint: Select the line-count option: wc -l document.txt
tasks.explanation: wc -l counts newline characters. Since every line here is newline-terminated, that equals the line count. Passing a filename prints the count and name; redirecting the file to stdin prints only the count.
